new.title: Climb the tower of Lausanne Cathedral
new.desc: Notre-Dame de Lausanne is a Gothic cathedral on the Cité hill, regarded as one of the finest in Switzerland. Its tower can be climbed for a panorama over the old town, the lake and the Alps. Part of the south transept and its rose window is under restoration until spring 2027.
new.tip: The tower climb costs about CHF 4 and the last ascent is 30 minutes before closing. Check the winter hours, which are shorter than the summer ones.
new.q: Cathédrale de Lausanne, Place de la Cathédrale, Lausanne

new.title: Admire Château Saint-Maire, seat of Vaud's government
new.desc: This brick and molasse-sandstone castle at the northern tip of the Cité hill was built from 1397 as the residence of the bishops of Lausanne. Since the creation of the canton it has housed the Vaud Council of State and the Chancellery. It is a Swiss heritage site of national importance.
new.tip: The interior is not open to the public, so admire the exterior and courtyard approaches. The cathedral belfry gives a good view of it from above.
new.q: Château Saint-Maire, Place du Château, Lausanne

new.title: Meet outsider art at the Collection de l'Art Brut
new.desc: Housed in the Château de Beaulieu, this museum grew from the collection that the painter Jean Dubuffet donated to Lausanne in 1971 and opened in 1976. It now holds tens of thousands of works by self-taught creators, which is the origin of the term art brut. Temporary exhibitions complement the permanent display.
new.tip: Open Tuesday to Sunday, with free entry on the first Saturday of the month. Buses 2, 3 and 21 stop at Beaulieu-Jomini.
new.q: Collection de l'Art Brut, Avenue des Bergières 11, Lausanne

new.title: Visit three museums at Plateforme 10
new.desc: Next to Lausanne station, Plateforme 10 brings together the Musée cantonal des Beaux-Arts (opened 2019), mudac for design and applied arts, and Photo Elysée, the cantonal photography museum (both in a building opened in June 2022). The architecture is by Barozzi Veiga and Aires Mateus.
new.tip: MCBA is closed on Mondays, mudac and Photo Elysée on Tuesdays. A combined ticket covers the three museums, and Thursday evening hours run later.
new.q: Plateforme 10, Place de la Gare 16, Lausanne

new.title: Explore the Olympic Museum and its lakeside park
new.desc: The Olympic Museum on the Quai d'Ouchy opened in 1993 together with its sculpture park, designed by José Lardet. It houses what is described as the largest Olympic heritage collection in the world, with tens of thousands of objects. The terrace and park look over Lake Geneva.
new.tip: Closed on Mondays in the low season. The M2 metro stops at Ouchy-Olympique, about five minutes' walk away; the park is free to enter.
new.q: Musée Olympique, Quai d'Ouchy 1, Lausanne

new.title: Climb the wooden Tour de Sauvabelin
new.desc: This 35-metre observation tower in the Sauvabelin forest was built in 2003 from Douglas fir cut in the city's own woods. A spiral of 302 steps leads to a 360-degree view of the lake, the Alps and the Jura. A free exhibition space sits at its foot.
new.tip: Free entry, open 8:00 to 20:00 in summer and to 17:00 in winter, closed in strong wind or ice. Bus 16 stops at Signal or Lac de Sauvabelin.
new.q: Tour de Sauvabelin, Chemin du Signal, Lausanne

new.title: Step inside the Palais de Rumine on Place de la Riponne
new.desc: This Florentine-style palace, built in the early 20th century with a bequest from Gabriel de Rumine, houses the cantonal university library and the Naturéum natural history museum. The cantonal museum of archaeology and history also sits inside, telling the story of Vaud from the Neolithic to today.
new.tip: The archaeology and history museum is open Tuesday to Sunday and is listed as free. The Wednesday and Saturday market takes place on the square in front.
new.q: Palais de Rumine, Place de la Riponne 6, Lausanne

new.title: See Château d'Ouchy, where the 1923 treaty was signed
new.desc: A bishop's fortress stood on this lakeshore from the Middle Ages, and the present neo-Gothic hotel was built in 1889-1893 around the surviving keep. A plaque commemorates the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne negotiated nearby. It is now a four-star hotel owned by the Sandoz Family Foundation.
new.tip: Walk past it along the Quais d'Ouchy; the terrace restaurant is open to non-guests. It stands a few steps from the CGN boat landing.
new.q: Château d'Ouchy, Place du Port 2, Lausanne

new.title: Walk the Roman town of Lousonna at Vidy
new.desc: The Roman museum stands on the ruins of a lavish 1st-century townhouse of the vicus of Lousonna, with its atrium, painted rooms and heated floors preserved. The current museum opened in 1993, and an archaeological park covers the old town centre alongside.
new.tip: Admission is from CHF 8 and free on the first Saturday of the month. Combine it with a walk on the nearby lake shore.
new.q: Musée romain de Lausanne-Vidy, Chemin du Bois-de-Vaud 24, Lausanne

new.title: Discover the Roman villa of Pully and its chariot fresco
new.desc: Excavations beginning in 1971 uncovered a large Roman villa from the early 2nd century at the Prieuré in Pully. It is known for a 15-metre semicircular fresco showing chariot races and for fragments of an upper-floor hexagonal mosaic. The site can be visited through the Pully archaeology programme.
new.tip: Visits are by opening days or guided tours, so check the Pully or Vaud archaeology pages before going. It is a short walk from the Pully priory church.
new.q: Villa romaine de Pully, Chemin du Prieuré, Pully

new.title: Order a moitié-moitié fondue at Café Romand
new.desc: A wood-panelled brasserie on Place Saint-François whose interior has been preserved since it opened in 1951. It is known for Vaud and Swiss classics such as papet vaudois, raclette and cheese fondue.
new.tip: Order the moitié-moitié fondue, which mixes Gruyère and Vacherin. It is busy and noisy, so book for groups.
new.q: Café Romand, Place Saint-François 2, Lausanne

new.title: Share a fondue at La Pinte Besson, Lausanne's oldest inn
new.desc: Reported as the city's oldest restaurant still operating and one of Europe's oldest bars, Pinte Besson was acquired in 1780 as a wine outlet in a vaulted cellar on rue de l'Ale. Most of the furnishings date from the early 20th century.
new.tip: Cheese fondue moitié-moitié is the speciality, with raclette and rösti also on the menu. Check hours first, as listings differ on Sunday opening.
new.q: La Pinte Besson, Rue de l'Ale 4, Lausanne

new.title: Have a terrace lunch at the Brasserie de Montbenon
new.desc: The brasserie occupies the rotunda of the Casino de Montbenon, dating from 1908 and renovated in 2014. Its terrace beside Montbenon park is one of the best-known in Lausanne for the view toward the lake.
new.tip: Come on a clear afternoon for the view. Weekends serve continuously from midday; book in summer.
new.q: Brasserie de Montbenon, Allée Ernest-Ansermet 3, Lausanne

new.title: Buy chocolate sticks at Blondel on Rue de Bourg
new.desc: Blondel has made chocolate in Lausanne since 1850. The Rue de Bourg boutique was restyled in 2019 to recall its oldest shop, and the chocolates are made by a small team just behind the shop.
new.tip: Try the hand-made truffles shaped like small sticks and the bars. Closed Sundays; Monday opening hours differ by listing.
new.q: Blondel Chocolatier, Rue de Bourg 5, Lausanne

new.title: Brunch at the Café de Grancy near the station
new.desc: This Café historique de Lausanne (a label created in 2021) sits in a late-19th-century building near the Ficelle. It serves a locavore brasserie menu in an art-deco setting and is known for its weekend brunch.
new.tip: Brunch is served Saturday and Sunday from about 10:00 to 15:00. Book ahead, as tables fill quickly.
new.q: Café de Grancy, Avenue du Rond-Point 1, Lausanne

new.title: Eat at the arty Bleu Lézard in the Flon
new.desc: An arty bistro on rue Enning founded in 1992, with a smaller underground bar called La Cave du Bleu. It serves brunch and a mix of bistro dishes at moderate prices.
new.tip: Main courses cost roughly CHF 20 to 30. It is popular for weekend brunch.
new.q: Le Bleu Lézard, Rue Enning 10, Lausanne

new.title: Taste Lavaux AOC wines at the Cave de Pully
new.desc: The commune of Pully runs its own vineyard of about 4 hectares and sells the wines, labelled Lavaux AOC, through the municipal cellar. White, rosé, red, sweet and sparkling wines are poured.
new.tip: Tastings of nine wines run on Thursdays from 17:00 to 20:00. Bottles can also be bought during office hours across from the cellar.
new.q: Cave de Pully, Avenue Samson-Reymondin 1, Pully

new.title: Stroll the Quais d'Ouchy from the old port to Tour Haldimand
new.desc: The lakeside promenade, built on reclaimed land between 1896 and 1901, is about a kilometre long and 30 metres wide. It links the old port with the Haldimand tower and passes Château d'Ouchy, the Olympic Museum and several parks, including a rose garden with over 130 kinds of roses.
new.tip: Busiest on Sundays. Pedal boats can be hired near the Denantou park, and the quays close to traffic during the October holidays.
new.q: Quais d'Ouchy, Quai d'Ouchy, Lausanne

new.title: Sail the Lavaux vineyards on a CGN boat from Ouchy
new.desc: The CGN lake steamers leave from the Ouchy pier on the Quai Jean-Pascal Delamuraz. The roughly three-hour Lavaux tour runs from Lausanne past the UNESCO-listed terraces to Vevey and back. Longer routes continue to Chillon and Montreux.
new.tip: Fares start around CHF 38 to 44 in second class. The nearest metro stop is Ouchy-Olympique, about five minutes' walk.
new.q: CGN Embarcadère Lausanne-Ouchy, Quai Jean-Pascal Delamuraz 1, Lausanne

new.title: Browse the Wednesday and Saturday market in the old town
new.desc: Lausanne's central food market runs on Wednesday and Saturday mornings through Riponne, rue Centrale, Place Saint-François and Place de la Palud. A non-food market with textiles, books and antiques is held in front of the Palais de Rumine.
new.tip: Go before 13:00, when stalls start closing. The Riponne metro stop is next to it.
new.q: Marché du centre-ville, Place de la Palud, Lausanne

new.title: Walk around the Lac de Sauvabelin
new.desc: This artificial lake in the Sauvabelin forest was created in 1889, and the paths, lake and playground were completely renovated in 2015-2017. The playground is the largest in Lausanne, and a ProSpecieRara animal park sits in the woods.
new.tip: Bus 16 stops at Lac de Sauvabelin. Combine it with a climb up the nearby wooden tower.
new.q: Lac de Sauvabelin, Chemin du Signal, Lausanne

new.title: Swim at the Bellerive-Plage lido
new.desc: Opened in 1937 and enlarged in 1964, Bellerive-Plage on the Vidy shore has an Olympic pool, a non-swimmer basin, diving boards and a supervised lake beach. It also has beach volleyball and basketball courts.
new.tip: Open from mid-May to mid-September. Entry to the pool is a few francs and the beach is reserved for paying pool users.
new.q: Bellerive-Plage, Avenue de Rhodanie 23, Lausanne

new.title: Wander the Flon, a former goods depot turned nightlife quarter
new.desc: The Flon was a stream used by craftsmen and later a freight yard, and it keeps cobblestones, old rails and the Voie-du-Chariot. It is now a district of bars, clubs, shops and terraces, with the open-air art Cubes. Both Lausanne metro lines run through it.
new.tip: Come at dusk, when bars and terraces fill up.
new.q: Quartier du Flon, Rue de Genève, Lausanne

new.title: Relax in the Parc de Mon Repos
new.desc: An English-style landscape garden whose villa was the headquarters of the International Olympic Committee from 1922 to 1967. The upper section has a neo-Gothic tower, a rock garden, a grotto and a tunnel in the romantic ruin style, and the park has a pool, aviaries and a restaurant.
new.tip: The park is free and shaded in summer. It is a short walk from the Olympic-era sights in the centre.
new.q: Parc de Mon Repos, Avenue de Mon-Repos, Lausanne

new.title: Ride the M2 metro from Ouchy up to the old town
new.desc: Lausanne's fully automated rubber-tyred M2 opened in October 2008 and reuses the old Métro-Ouchy rack line. It climbs from the lakeshore at Ouchy-Olympique through about 6 km of the city to the Croisettes terminus, with gradients of up to 12 percent.
new.tip: Buy a ticket valid for zones 11 and 12 or use the Lausanne Transport Card. Ride from Ouchy to Flon for an easy way up from the lake.
new.q: Métro M2 Ouchy-Olympique, Place de la Navigation 6, Lausanne

new.title: Explore Château de Chillon on the lake
new.desc: This island-style castle between Montreux and Villeneuve served as a Savoyard stronghold and a prison, famed for the cell of François Bonivard. Visitors see dungeons, halls and towers with views of the lake and Alps.
new.tip: Reach it by boat, train to Veytaux-Chillon or bus. It is closed on 25 December and 1 January; allow two hours.
new.q: Château de Chillon, Avenue de Chillon 21, Veytaux

new.title: Pay your respects at the Freddie Mercury statue
new.desc: A three-metre bronze by the Czech sculptor Irena Sedlecká, unveiled in 1996, stands on the Montreux lakeside promenade at Place du Marché. Fans leave flowers at its feet all year round.
new.tip: Free and open at any time. Special tributes take place around 5 September, Mercury's birthday.
new.q: Statue de Freddie Mercury, Place du Marché, Montreux

new.title: Visit the Alimentarium food museum in Vevey
new.desc: Founded by Nestlé, the Alimentarium is a museum of food and nutrition in a neoclassical lakeside building that once held Nestlé's headquarters. Its exhibitions, garden and terrace cover food from historical, scientific and cultural angles.
new.tip: Closed on Mondays. Workshops for children are offered.
new.q: Alimentarium, Quai Perdonnet 25, Vevey

new.title: Photograph La Fourchette, the giant fork in the lake
new.desc: A stainless-steel fork rises from Lake Geneva a few metres from Quai Perdonnet in front of the Alimentarium. Neuchâtel artist Jean-Pierre Zaugg made it for the museum's tenth anniversary in 1995, and it has been listed as the world's tallest fork.
new.tip: Free to see from the quay at any time. Combine with the nearby Chaplin statue and promenade.
new.q: La Fourchette, Quai Perdonnet, Vevey

new.title: See prints and paintings at the Musée Jenisch
new.desc: This neoclassical museum was inaugurated in 1897 after a bequest from Fanny Jenisch and fully renovated in 2012. It houses the cantonal print cabinet with over 40,000 works from the Renaissance to the present, plus fine art exhibitions.
new.tip: Check the current exhibition on museejenisch.ch. It is next to Vevey station.
new.q: Musée Jenisch Vevey, Avenue de la Gare 2, Vevey

new.title: Play in the castle of La Tour-de-Peilz at the Swiss Games Museum
new.desc: The 13th-century castle built under Peter of Savoy served for defence and customs and was bought by the commune in 1979. The Musée suisse du jeu, opened in 1987, fills its upper floor and attic with games from antiquity to video games.
new.tip: Open Tuesday to Sunday from 11:00 to 17:30. Entry is inexpensive, from CHF 3 to 9.
new.q: Château de La Tour-de-Peilz, Rue du Château 11, La Tour-de-Peilz

new.title: Wander the medieval bourg of Lutry
new.desc: Lutry's old town began to grow soon after the year 1000 around a Benedictine priory. A bishop's castle and ramparts followed in the 14th century. The Saint-Martin-et-Saint-Clément church stands at the centre, with the Lavaux terraces behind.
new.tip: Take the S31 train from Lausanne. Lutry is also the start of the Lavaux Express and the Lutry to Saint-Saphorin walk.
new.q: Bourg de Lutry, Rue du Bourg, Lutry

new.title: Stroll through the fortified village of Saint-Saphorin
new.desc: This winegrowing village in Lavaux is mentioned in a document of 1138. Arcades built to carry the house facades guard against landslides, and it has been one of the Most Beautiful Villages in Switzerland since 2016.
new.tip: Reach it by train on the S31. It is a good lunch stop on the Lavaux walk.
new.q: Saint-Saphorin (Lavaux), Rue du Village, Saint-Saphorin

new.title: Take in the view from Vevey's Saint-Martin church
new.desc: The Reformed Saint-Martin church stands on a terrace above Vevey, and its tower is visible from afar. The terrace offers views over the town, Lake Geneva and the Alps.
new.tip: Check whether the interior is open before climbing. The terrace is a quiet spot above the old town.
new.q: Église Saint-Martin, Boulevard Saint-Martin, Vevey

new.title: Spot the 13th-century Tour de Marsens in the Dézaley vines
new.desc: This four-storey tower on a steep slope above Dézaley is documented from 1272 and gives its name to a Dézaley Grand Cru. It rises from the vineyards just after Epesses.
new.tip: The tower sits on private land, so view it from the Lavaux paths. Komoot loops from Chexbres pass it.
new.q: Tour de Marsens, Dézaley, Puidoux

new.title: Dine on rotisserie dishes at the Auberge de l'Onde
new.desc: A brasserie and rotisserie in Saint-Saphorin, where meat and fish are grilled in the fireplace beneath old beams. Gault & Millau gave it 15 points, and its sommelier is known for Swiss wines, especially Lavaux chasselas.
new.tip: Open Wednesday to Sunday. Book a table and ask for a Lavaux chasselas; the lunch menu is the cheaper option.
new.q: Auberge de l'Onde, Chemin Neuf 2, Saint-Saphorin

new.title: Taste Lavaux wines at the Caveau des Vignerons de Cully
new.desc: About ten Cully winemakers take turns pouring a selection of about thirty wines at this caveau in the Lavaux UNESCO vineyard. Tasting formats include wine and chocolate pairings.
new.tip: Open roughly Thursday to Sunday evenings from 17:00 to 21:00 in season. Confirm the hours before going.
new.q: Caveau des Vignerons de Cully, Place d'Armes 16, Cully

new.title: Taste Dézaley Médinette at Domaine Louis Bovard
new.desc: The Bovard family winery in Cully farms about 18 hectares across several Lavaux communes. Its best-known wine is the Dézaley Grand Cru Médinette, a chasselas that has scored 92 to 95 points in recent vintages.
new.tip: The vinothèque at Place d'Armes receives walk-in tastings, but confirm hours first.
new.q: Domaine Louis Bovard, Place d'Armes 2, Cully

new.title: Dine on the terrace of Le Deck at Baron Tavernier
new.desc: Le Deck, the restaurant of Le Baron Tavernier hotel above Chexbres, has a terrace overlooking Lavaux, the lake and the Alps. Lausanne Tourisme calls the view arguably the best in the canton.
new.tip: The terrace is open from spring to autumn; in winter eat at Le Baron or the Bon Sauvage bistro. Book for sunset.
new.q: Le Baron Tavernier, Route de la Corniche 4, Chexbres

new.title: Try fondue and perch fillets at Les Trois Sifflets
new.desc: A well-known old-town address in Vevey, a few steps from Place de l'Hôtel de Ville, serving Vaud classics such as fondue, cheese crust and perch fillets. Staff serve the fondue in Swiss Army uniforms.
new.tip: Order the fondue or filets de perche, the lake's speciality. Perch is best in autumn and winter.
new.q: Café des Trois Sifflets, Vevey

new.title: Eat fondue in the glass Fondue Tube above Montreux
new.desc: The Fondue Tube at the Eurotel Montreux is a glass-enclosed terrace with an open view of Lake Geneva and the Alps. Cheese fondue is its speciality.
new.tip: Book ahead for a table with the view. Check the season and hours before going.
new.q: Eurotel Montreux Fondue Tube, Grand-Rue 81, Montreux

new.title: Order lake perch at the J5 brasserie in Montreux
new.desc: The J5 brasserie in the Hôtel Helvétie serves perch fillets sourced from a local fisherman in Villeneuve. It celebrates the lake in its cooking.
new.tip: Order the filets de perche. Check opening hours and book on weekends.
new.q: J5 Brasserie, Hôtel Helvétie, Rue du Théâtre 5, Montreux

new.title: Taste Chablais AOC wines at Domaine Bertholet in Villeneuve
new.desc: A family winery in Villeneuve, in the Chablais Vaudois wine area, run by Christophe Bertholet. All wines sold carry the Chablais AOC label, and the estate offers tastings and cellar visits.
new.tip: Tasting experiences cost roughly CHF 43 to 65. Book ahead.
new.q: Domaine Bertholet, Rue des Fortifications 29, Villeneuve

new.title: Ride the cogwheel train to Rochers-de-Naye
new.desc: The MOB rack railway climbs from Montreux through Glion and Caux to the 2,042-metre summit in about 50 minutes. The top station has a hotel, restaurants, a marmot enclosure and, in summer, the free La Rambertia alpine garden.
new.tip: Sit on the right side going up. Dress warmly, as the summit is much colder than the lake.
new.q: Rochers-de-Naye, Gare de Montreux, Avenue des Alpes, Montreux

new.title: Visit Chaplin's World at the Manoir de Ban
new.desc: Charlie Chaplin lived at the Manoir de Ban in Corsier-sur-Vevey from 1953 until his death in 1977. The museum opened in April 2016 and includes the manor, a park and a film studio.
new.tip: Check opening hours at chaplinsworld.com. Allow at least half a day.
new.q: Chaplin's World, Route de Fenil 2, Corsier-sur-Vevey

new.title: Hike the Lavaux terraces from Lutry to Saint-Saphorin
new.desc: A waymarked walk of about 11 km crosses the Lutry, Villette and Epesses wine zones, climbing through Cully and Epesses before descending to Rivaz and Saint-Saphorin. The vineyard has been UNESCO-listed since 2007.
new.tip: Take the S31 train back from Rivaz or Saint-Saphorin. Allow about three hours, and wear sturdy shoes.
new.q: Gare de Cully, Cully

new.title: Shop at Vevey's market on the Grande Place
new.desc: A renowned market takes place on the Grande Place in Vevey on Tuesday and Saturday mornings. On summer Saturdays the square also hosts a folklore market.
new.tip: Check vevey.ch for current layout. Go in the morning.
new.q: Grande Place, Vevey

new.title: Walk the flower-lined Quai des Fleurs in Montreux
new.desc: The Montreux lakeside promenade is nicknamed Quai des Fleurs because palms, cypresses and exotic flowers grow in the mild climate. The Montreux Jazz Festival has been held along it since 1967.
new.tip: Walk from Villeneuve to Montreux, about three hours round trip, or stroll the central stretch by the Freddie Mercury statue.
new.q: Quai des Fleurs, Quai de la Rouvenaz, Montreux

new.title: Browse the Montreux Noël Christmas market
new.desc: Montreux Noël fills the lakeside quays, Grand-Rue and Place du Marché from 20 November to 24 December 2026. Entry is free, and paid extras include the Santa's House at Rochers-de-Naye and flying Santa cruise.
new.tip: The market closes at 17:00 on 24 December. Check montreuxnoel.com for the programme.
new.q: Montreux Noël, Place du Marché, Montreux

new.title: Ride the Lavaux Express train through the vines
new.desc: This tourist train runs two loops of about 1h15 in the UNESCO vineyards, one from Lutry through Aran and Grandvaux and one from Cully through Riex, Epesses and the Dézaley. The Cully loop stops at Dézaley for a view and a tasting.
new.tip: Runs roughly April to early November, with departures from Cully or Lutry on alternate days. Book ahead on lavauxexpress.ch.
new.q: Lavaux Express, Place d'Armes, Cully
